posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value ICP prospects engaging on a compliance/explainability pain post — validate the 'GPT said so' problem with a specific observation about auditability, not AI itself
posts.draft_comment: The ban is rarely about the AI. It's about whether anyone in the room can trace the number back to a source when the pressure's on. Regulators don't want confidence intervals, they want a paper trail. The question worth asking isn't 'can we use AI?' — it's 'can we defend what it produced?'

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with adoption failure after 18 months of Power BI build — validate the pain, add the trust-gap insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The dirty secret is that dashboards don't fail on data quality, they fail on provenance. Finance teams need to know *why* a number is what it is before they'll say it out loud in a board meeting — and most tools just show the answer without showing the working. Eighteen months to build, probably another eighteen to earn that trust. Did anyone on the project ever ask the finance team what would actually make them confident enough to quote it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why 10% usage happens in the first place' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is usually a politics problem disguised as a data problem — everyone fought to get their metric on the dashboard, so nothing got cut. The jump to 85% usage tells you people weren't disengaged, they just couldn't find themselves in it. I think the hard part isn't building the five metrics, it's getting the room to agree which five actually matter. How long did that conversation take?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI failure — validate the 'who owns the truth' framing, add the insight that the problem isn't access to data, it's the absence of shared definitions baked into the tool itself
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so real. Everyone's technically empowered and yet somehow no one trusts any number enough to say it out loud in a meeting. I think the mistake was assuming that giving people access to data was the same as giving them a shared understanding of it — those are completely different problems. Who in your org is actually allowed to say 'this is the number'?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing hallucinations as a security risk, with a CEO ICP prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust/accountability layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I don't think most AI analytics vendors are ready for it. A wrong number in a dashboard is embarrassing. A hallucinated number in a board-level financial report that drives a capital decision — that's a different category of problem entirely. Who in your org actually owns that accountability chain right now?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person firm nailing the exact pain Milo solves, with a COO ICP prospect engaging — validate the £200k waste pattern, add the 'built for builders not business' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is almost always followed by the same sentence: 'yeah, but only Dave really uses it.' The tool gets bought by someone technical, built by someone technical, and then handed to a finance director who just needs to know if Q3 is on track. The vendors know this and sell to the data team anyway because that's who's in the room. Makes you wonder if 'self-service' was ever meant for the business, or just meant to sound like it was.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director calling out a data governance/culture problem that BI tools keep failing to solve — validate the diagnosis and add the layer most people skip over
posts.draft_comment: The filter problem is almost never accidental. Three teams building their own version of the truth is usually a signal that nobody agreed on what the truth was supposed to look like in the first place — before anyone opened a BI tool. Culture fix is right, but it has to happen upstream of the dashboard, not as a reaction to it. How long did it take to figure out which team's numbers were actually correct?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with shadow AI as the punchline — validate the usage gap insight and reframe the problem as 'knowing what to ask' before any tool can help
posts.draft_comment: The 12% stat doesn't surprise me — most rollouts treat AI adoption like a software install problem when it's actually a question literacy problem. People don't know what to ask because they don't have a clear picture of what's worth asking about in the first place. Shadow AI filling that gap with ChatGPT on phones is just people finding the path of least resistance. What does the 12% who are using it actually have in common?
